The curves intersect when $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \frac{4\pi}{3}$. Region $R$ is in the second quadrant, bordered by each curve and the y-axis. ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure has rectangular coordinate axes and a grid; on the left is a circular curve labeled \(r=-3\cos\theta\), and on the right is a curve labeled \(r=2+\cos\theta\); the two curves have one intersection point each at the upper left and lower left. The label \(R\) in the figure is located at the upper left, between the two curves, near the \(y\)-axis, so there is a tension in expression between the text's "second quadrant, bounded by the \(y\)-axis and the two curves" and the complete region between the two intersection points represented by the given standard integral. Reasoning: To remain consistent with the two intersection points \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}\) and \(\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3}\) given in the problem and with the verified answer, set up the integral according to the region between the two curves swept from the upper intersection point to the lower intersection point. On \([\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3}]\), \(\cos\theta\le -\frac12\), so \(-3\cos\theta\ge 2+\cos\theta\); for example, when \(\theta=\pi\), \(-3\cos\pi=3\), while \(2+\cos\pi=1\). Therefore the outer radius is \(r=-3\cos\theta\), and the inner radius is \(r=2+\cos\theta\). By the formula for the area between two curves in polar coordinates, the area can be set as \(\frac{1}{2}\int_{\frac{2\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left((-3\cos\theta)^2-(2+\cos\theta)^2\right)d\theta\).
